newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao appeals to High Court on bail.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao appeals to High Court on bail.

text.p: Former Indian Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao appealed on Tuesday to the Delhi High Court after a magistrate dismissed his bail application in a criminal forgery case, his lawyers said.
"We are moving the High Court to appeal against the order of Prem Kumar," lawyer R.K. Anand told reporters, referring to the Chief Metropolitian Magistrate.
Later, another member of the legal team said the appeal had been lodged but no date had been set for the hearing.
Kumar dismissed regular bail applications by Rao, 75, former minister K.K. Tewary and two other people charged in the case.
He gave Rao and Tewary until November 14 to appeal to a higher court. The two others are already in detention for a separate case.

"After most careful circumspection, I am of the view that in the larger interest of the state and fair trial of the case the accused persons are not entitled to bail at this stage of the case," Kumar said in a written order.
In the case, Rao already has anticipatory bail, allowed under Indian law to pre-empt possible arrest until a trial begins. Later, the bail has to be decided by the trial courts.
Rao is the first former or serving prime minister to face criminal charges. He resigned as prime minister in May after his Congress party was mauled in general elections.
If denied bail by a higher court, Rao, who has also been charged in a separate case of bribery, could be arrested and taken into custody, legal experts said.

In September, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) charged Rao with aiding the alleged defamation in 1989 of V.P. Singh, a Congress defector who later became prime minister, with the help of forged papers showing an illegal bank account.
Rao has not commented publicly on the case, whose charges carry a maximum sentence of seven years in jail.
Rao appeared twice in court last week in the case, one of the three in which he is facing a court summons or trial.
Kumar said he refused Rao's bail application to prevent any obstruction of evidence in the case.
"The personalities involved are not men of straw or ordinary mortals," he said.

As the judge read out his order, Rao sat grimly in the courtroom, specially set up at Vigyan Bhavan, a conference centre, after security experts had ruled the normal courthouse venue was not safe from separatist threats.
Rao, who was in court for only three minutes, was surrounded by leaders of the Congress party.
Apart from Rao and Tewary, the other two accused are Chandraswami, a Hindu guru close to Rao and the guru's assistant, Kailash Nath Agarwal. Both are in jail.
The four are alleged to have acted in collusion to show that Singh's son held $21 million in a bank account on the Caribbean island of St Kitts.

Rao was also scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday in a separate cheating case involving an expatriate Indian businessman who claimed he paid $100,000 to a Rao acquaintance in 1983 in a failed attempt to win a government contract.
Rao resigned in September as president of the Congress party, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence from Britain in 1947.

He is also facing charges in a vote-buying scandal, in which the CBI accuses Rao and senior party colleagues of playing a role in buying a crucial parliamentary vote of confidence in 1993, which Rao's minority government won by a thin margin.
